title: Amend the vacuous-uniformity profile section with its third instance and the actionable remedy
description:
opum-agent reported a third instance of the trap QCLI-341 recorded, collected by falling into it twenty minutes after reading the close-out, while writing the dispatch about it. Two things in their report are not covered by the section as written.

FIRST, A SUB-CASE THE SECTION MISSES. QCLI-341 covers a field that does not exist anywhere. Their instance was a WRONG NESTING LEVEL: quest task view <id> --json piped to jq selecting id, title, status returned a uniform null because the record is under .data and every key named was absent at the TOP level. The field exists; the path pointed one level too high. The section recommends has() and grepping the producing source, and neither helps when you are querying the wrong object -- has() on the wrong object is just as uniformly false.

SECOND, A SHARPER REMEDY, and it is theirs: print the key set. Their words, and the reason to prefer it: be careful with nulls is not actionable and print the key set is. Dumping the top-level keys is what caught it, and it covers both sub-cases where presence-testing a named key covers only one.

Also worth recording because it bears on what this section can achieve: they were carrying a private note on this exact trap and had just read a handoff naming it, and hit it anyway. That is the third data point for the section admitting it is an artifact and not a control.

The product half of this is already fixed separately as QCLI-342, which put the remedy into the overview guide where far more readers see it. This task is the profile half only.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The profile section covers the wrong-nesting-level sub-case as distinct from the field-does-not-exist case, and says why has() and grep do not catch it
The remedy names printing the key set, attributed to opum-agent, with the reason that it covers both sub-cases where a named-key presence test covers one
The third instance is recorded with the detail that makes it evidence rather than an anecdote: it was hit by someone carrying a note about it, minutes after reading a handoff naming it
The section cross-references QCLI-342 so a reader knows the product guide already carries the remedy, and the edit changes no managed block

implementationNotes: THE SUB-CASE IS THE SUBSTANTIVE ADDITION, not the anecdote. QCLI-341 recorded one way to get a uniform null (the field exists nowhere) and prescribed two checks for it, has() and grepping the producer. Their instance is the OTHER way: the field exists and the path points at the wrong object. Both prescribed checks fail on it -- has("id") on the envelope is equally false, and grepping for id finds it everywhere. So the section as written would have been read by someone in exactly their situation and would have sent them to two checks that both confirm the wrong conclusion. The key-set line now leads because it is the only one covering both.

CONFINEMENT: 35 insertions, 0 deletions on CLAUDE.md, so no existing line was touched. quest agents --check --require-installed --target claude exits 0. lore check exits 0 across 63 files. No source or test files in the diff -- the product half of this shipped separately as QCLI-342.
finalSummary:
Amended the vacuous-uniformity profile section with the sub-case it missed, the remedy that covers both, and the third instance.

THE SUBSTANTIVE GAP, and it was not cosmetic. QCLI-341 recorded ONE way to get a uniform null -- the field exists nowhere -- and prescribed has() plus grepping the producer. opum-agents instance is the OTHER way: the field exists and the path points at the wrong object (quest task view piped to jq selecting id, title, status, all null, because the record is under .data). BOTH prescribed checks fail on it: has("id") on the envelope is equally false, and grepping for id finds it everywhere. So the section as written would have sent someone in exactly their situation to two checks that each confirm the wrong conclusion. That is worse than an incomplete section; it is a misleading one.

THE REMEDY, theirs, now leading the block: print the key set. Their reason is the right one -- be careful with nulls is not a check, print the key set is -- and it is the only line covering both sub-cases where a named-key presence test covers one.

THE THIRD INSTANCE IS RECORDED AS EVIDENCE, not colour, because of the specific circumstances: they hit it twenty minutes after reading the close-out recording it, while writing the dispatch to spread it fleet-wide, carrying a private note on the same trap, having just read a handoff naming it as one of three errors its predecessor made in ninety minutes. Three sessions, all of whom knew the rule. The section now states plainly that it is an artifact and not a control, names the mechanical version that would be one (a lint over evidence-bearing prose for field names absent from the producing source), records that nobody has commissioned it, and records the agreed trigger for revisiting: a fourth instance after the fleet-level record lands.

Also recorded: the cost is not abstract. Believing the all-null would have meant re-filing a task that already existed, and this tracker mints the next id on create, so the recovery from the wrong conclusion produces a duplicate record.

SCOPE. Profile half only. The product half shipped separately as QCLI-342, which corrected the overview guide -- itself found to be documenting the envelope without contractVersion -- and put the key-set remedy where far more readers see it. The section cross-references it.

VERIFIED. 35 insertions and ZERO deletions on CLAUDE.md, so no existing line was touched. quest agents --check --require-installed --target claude exits 0. lore check exits 0 across 63 files. No source or test files in the diff.
